R008_after6.caption:
You logged off at 6. So why are you still answering your boss at 10? 👀

Dinner gets cold.
The show gets paused.
One more "quick one" before tomorrow.

Then "quick" turns into an hour, every night.

It's not just you: Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index found the average worker sends or receives 50+ messages outside core hours.

In healthy workplaces, after-hours is for emergencies.
In toxic ones, it's just more hours.

So set your hours once, in writing, while you're calm: "I'm offline after 6. I'll handle this first thing tomorrow." Then turn on Do Not Disturb.
That's not lazy. It's a boundary.

Does YOUR boss expect replies after hours? 👇

Send this to the 10 PM replier.

R009_mondays.caption:
You used to love this job. So why do you dread Mondays now? 👀

Sunday night, your stomach starts to turn.
Monday, there's a 1:1 on the calendar.
The agenda just says "we need to talk."

You start wondering if the problem is you.

Often it's not. Gallup found managers account for at least 70% of the variance in team engagement.

In healthy teams, a good manager makes hard work feel doable.
In toxic ones, a bad manager makes good work feel impossible.

You can't fix your boss. But you can control three things: ask for every 1:1 agenda ahead of time, write down your wins each week, and talk to another team this month.
That's not giving up. It's protecting your energy.

Is it the job, or is it YOUR boss? 👇

Send this to someone who dreads Mondays.

C003_sayno.caption:
Your boss asks for one more thing. So why can't you just say no? 👀

Your plate is already full.
The deadline is already tight.
And "no" still feels like a risk.

So you say yes, and stay late again.

You're not imagining the pressure: in APA's 2023 Work in America Survey, 19% of U.S. workers called their workplace toxic.

A flat "no" can backfire.
A silent "yes" burns you out.

Try one of these instead:
"Happy to. Which project should move so I can fit this in?"
"Not today, but Friday works."
"I'm at capacity. Can we revisit Monday?"
That's not difficult. It's professional.

Which script would YOU use first? 👇

Save these for your next ask, and send them to the coworker who never says no.
